paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Solubility is the ability of one substance, the solute, to form a solution with another, the solvent. Its opposite, insolubility, is the inability to form such a solution. A solute may be solid, liquid or gaseous, while the solvent is usually a solid or a liquid.

paragraphs.heading: Saturation and balance
paragraphs.text: Solubility is usually measured as the concentration of solute in a saturated solution, one that cannot dissolve any more. At that point the two substances are at the solubility equilibrium. This balance is dynamic. Dissolving and its reverse, such as a solid coming back out as a precipitate, go on at the same time, and a stable state is reached when their rates are equal.

paragraphs.heading: Mixing without limit
paragraphs.text: Some pairs have no limit at all and are called miscible, meaning they mix in all proportions. Gases are always miscible with each other, except in very extreme situations. Solubility ranges from ethanol in water, which mixes without limit, to titanium dioxide, which is essentially insoluble in water.

paragraphs.heading: What controls it
paragraphs.text: Solubility depends mainly on what the solute and solvent are made of, including their pH and any other dissolved substances, and on temperature and pressure. These effects can often be explained by how the particles of the two substances interact, and by thermodynamic ideas such as enthalpy and entropy. Solubility also differs from the rate of solution, meaning how fast a solid dissolves in a liquid. That rate depends on other things, such as the physical form of the substances and how hard they are mixed.

paragraphs.heading: Going past the limit
paragraphs.text: Under certain conditions a solution can hold more solute than its usual limit. The result is called a supersaturated solution. It will quickly push out the extra solute once a suitable nucleation site appears.

paragraphs.heading: How it is written
paragraphs.text: Chemical handbooks often give solubility as grams of solute per 100 mL of solvent, or as grams per 100 g of solvent. It can also be given in moles, for example as moles of solute per litre of solution, the molarity. Converting between these units can be tricky, because it may call for the density of the solution, a figure that often goes unmeasured.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Solubility matters well beyond chemistry, in fields such as geology, biology, medicine and agriculture, and even in cooking, cleaning and brewing. Most useful chemical reactions only take place after the ingredients have been dissolved in a suitable solvent. Water is by far the most common choice.
